title: Mitigating Conversational Inertia in Multi-Turn Agents
one_liner: Reduce the tendency to repeat the agent's own earlier replies by training preferences that favor fresher actions when the state is the same.
lead: This paper studies a subtle multi-turn agent failure. After several turns, the model may start copying the style and action pattern of its own earlier responses even when the environment now calls for a different move. The paper names that problem conversational inertia and proposes Context Preference Learning, which prefers responses from shorter, less self-reinforcing contexts when the current state is otherwise the same.

problem.h2: Why long conversations can trap an agent in its own past
paras: A multi-turn agent should use the growing conversation to gather more evidence from the environment. But the same history can become a trap because the model may treat its own earlier replies as examples to imitate rather than as actions that should be reconsidered.

That hurts exploration. If the agent keeps echoing its previous response pattern, it may stop trying new actions even after the environment shows that the old plan is failing. The paper studies this effect and asks how to bias the model toward lower-inertia actions without needing environment reward labels for every pair.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Compare actions produced from shorter and longer contexts for the same state, then train the model to prefer the action that is less trapped by its own conversation history.

panels.title: 1. The agent starts a search
panels.viz_args: It can inspect the environment, choose tools, and revise the plan.
panels.caption: Early in the run, several next actions are still possible because the conversation has not hardened into one pattern.

panels.title: 2. The history grows
panels.viz_args: The context now contains many earlier replies from the same agent.
panels.caption: Those earlier replies can dominate because the model keeps seeing its own wording and action style.

panels.title: 3. The agent repeats itself
panels.viz_args: It keeps issuing the same kind of move even when the environment changed.
panels.caption: This is inertia because the model imitates its own past instead of responding to the present state.

panels.title: 4. Preference training reverses the bias
panels.viz_args: When the same state is shown, shorter-context actions can be preferred if they stay more open to new moves.
panels.caption: The method works by using context length as a source of preference pairs.

panels.title: 5. The agent explores again
panels.caption: Later actions become less repetitive because the model is trained to resist copying its own earlier replies.

steps.text: Construct comparisons where the environment state is the same so differences mainly reflect the conversation history.
Ask the model for actions with shorter and longer histories because the longer history tends to carry more self-copying pressure.

Treat the lower-inertia action as preferred so the model can be trained without hand-labeled environment rewards for every case because matched short-context and long-context outputs already supply a comparison signal.
Update the model toward lower-inertia actions because those actions leave more room to respond to fresh environmental evidence.
Trim or structure the context so useful feedback stays available while extra self-repetition pressure stays lower.

paras: The paper changes the agent's preference over candidate next actions. It tries to make the model value actions that are less driven by its own earlier replies when the present state does not justify repeating them.
object.object: the next-action preference inside a multi-turn agent

hidden.name: how strongly the next action is pulled by the agent's own earlier replies instead of the current state
paras: The hidden quantity is self-copying pressure from the conversation history. You cannot read that pressure directly from one sentence, but you can infer it when the same state produces a more repetitive action under a longer context than under a shorter one.

That comparison gives the paper a practical training signal. If the shorter-context action reacts better to the current state, then the longer-context action reveals excess inertia because the extra history changed the action even though the state stayed fixed.

heat.caption: The dark cells mark places where history pressure can overwhelm present evidence and keep the agent repeating itself.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is whether the next move comes from the current situation or from the agent copying its own earlier replies.
The method estimates conversational inertia by comparing actions under matched states with different context lengths, then learns to prefer the lower-inertia action.

mechanism.h2: Why comparing shorter and longer contexts gives a training signal
paras: The core observation is that context length changes the amount of self-copying pressure even when the state is the same. That is useful because the method can harvest preference pairs from the model's own behavior instead of waiting for delayed environment rewards.

Context management then supports the learned preference at runtime. Keeping the most relevant environment feedback while trimming excess self-history helps because the agent still sees the current task evidence but sees fewer repeated traces of its own old plan.

stages.s: One state paired with short and long conversation histories
Prefer the action less dominated by history
Train and trim context during execution
A multi-turn agent that stays more responsive to new evidence

math.words: One simple way to think about the method is to reward actions that respond to the present state and penalize actions that mostly repeat the prior conversation pattern.
symbols: value of one candidate next action
how well the action matches the current environment state
penalty when the action is mainly driven by copying the earlier conversation

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: The state now shows that the first search path failed.
Action A repeats the old plan, so state_fit is 3 and inertia_cost is 5.
Action B opens a new search path, so state_fit is 8 and inertia_cost is 1.
Preference training should favor B because B reacts to the current evidence instead of copying the stale plan.

math.note: The paper uses preference learning rather than this exact formula, but the formula captures the tradeoff between present-state fit and self-copying pressure.

charts.title: Long history without correction
charts.note: Performance drops because the model keeps reusing earlier reply patterns instead of adapting to the current situation.

charts.title: Context Preference Learning
charts.note: The paper reports better agent performance because the model is trained to resist excess inertia and remain more responsive to new evidence.

items.b: Shorter context is not always better.
items.html: If important earlier evidence is removed, the agent can make a worse choice because the shorter context hid facts that the current state alone does not contain.
Two actions may differ for reasons other than inertia, so the training signal can be imperfect because context length is only a proxy for the true cause.
An agent should repeat a good plan when the environment still supports it, so anti-inertia training must not punish justified consistency.
The paper is useful because it turns a subtle conversational failure into a trainable preference signal.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a multi-turn search task where the environment occasionally reveals that the current plan failed and a new plan is needed. Generate candidate actions for the same state under shorter and longer conversation histories, then train one agent with those preference pairs and leave another agent unchanged.

The demo should show that the trained agent changes course sooner after new evidence appears because it is less trapped by its own earlier replies, while the unchanged agent keeps repeating stale actions for longer.
demo.closing: A convincing demo shows better adaptation because the next action is driven more by the current state and less by copied history.
